This vignette opens the machine. Nothing here is needed to *use* the
package; it is for the reader who wants to know what is being computed, and
why the answers carry an accounting of floating-point adjustments.

## Expected hits and the running remainder

Write $\lambda_i$ for the expected number of selections (*hits*) of unit
$i$, in list order, with $\sum_i \lambda_i = n$, the sample size. Split each
$\lambda_i$ into its integer part $k_i$ and fractional part $r_i$. The
integer parts are guaranteed: unit $i$ will be selected at least $k_i$
times. The procedure's whole business is the fractional parts.

Walk the list accumulating the fractional parts: $F_i = F_{i-1} + r_i$,
wrapping to $F_i - 1$ whenever the sum crosses one. Each crossing releases
one further selection, to be given either to the unit where the crossing
happened or to a unit after it. Because every $r_i < 1$, no unit can
receive more than one of these released selections — which is why each
unit's hits are $k_i$ or $k_i + 1$ and never further from $\lambda_i$:
*probability minimum replacement*.

## The transition probabilities

What makes the procedure correct, and not merely clever, is the conditional
draw at each unit. Let $T_{i-1}$ be the selections made so far and
$I_{i-1}$ the selections *available* so far (the accumulated integer parts
plus crossings). At unit $i$ there is at most one selection pending —
$T_{i-1}$ is either $I_{i-1}$ or $I_{i-1} - 1$ — and Chromy gives the
probability that unit $i$ settles it, conditional on the state:

| state at $i-1$ | crossing at $i$ | probability unit $i$'s extra hit occurs |
|---|---|---|
| nothing pending | no  | $r_i / (1 - F_{i-1})$ |
| nothing pending | yes | $0$ |
| one pending     | no  | $1$ |
| one pending     | yes | $F_i / F_{i-1}$ |

One uniform per unit decides it. These conditionals are built so that,
unconditionally, each unit's extra hit has probability exactly $r_i$ — the
procedure is a sequential implementation of the design, not an
approximation to it. Chauvet and Le Gleut (2021) give the formal
properties, including the joint inclusion probabilities.

You can watch the state machine directly: the engine reports the hits and
the accounting of the walk.


``` r
library(chromy)
frame <- data.frame(size = c(2.0, 0.6, 1.4, 0.3, 0.7))
s <- chromy_sample(frame, n = 5, size = "size",
                   min_replacement = TRUE, seed = 1)
s$sample[c("unit", "expected_hits", "fixed_hits", "random_hits", "hits")]
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>    unit expected_hits fixed_hits random_hits  hits
#>   <int>         <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1           2            2           0     2
#> 2     2           0.6          0           1     1
#> 3     3           1.4          1           0     1
#> 4     4           0.3          0           1     1
```

Unit 1, expected 2 times, carries its fixed hits; the
fractional parts are settled one crossing at a time.

## The head of the list

Run from a fixed first unit, the procedure would treat the units near the
head subtly differently from the units near the tail. Chromy's remedy, kept
by SAS and by this package, is to draw the head itself with probability
proportional to size and rotate the list to start there. With
`head = "residual"`, only units with a fractional expected hit may be drawn
as the head, and the integer hits are taken as fixed.

## The floating-point accounting

The arithmetic above is exact over the reals and approximate over doubles,
and a sampling procedure cannot shrug at the difference: a remainder that
lands at $1 - 10^{-16}$ either is or is not a crossing, and the answer
changes who can be selected. The engine does three things about it, and
reports all three rather than hiding them:

1. **The drift is measured.** The expected hits are summed with compensated
   (Kahan) arithmetic; the difference between the sum and the integer $n$
   must be below $10^{-8}$, or the selection is refused — silently rescaling
   the caller's probabilities would detach the weights from the design.
2. **The drift is assigned.** One unit — the largest fractional part that
   can absorb it — takes the whole correction, so every other unit's
   probability is exactly what the caller asked.
3. **Near-boundary crossings are settled.** A remainder within four units
   in the last place of 1 is treated as a crossing, the missing sliver
   borrowed from the units that follow.

The `accounting` element of the sample says what was done; the
`expected_hits` on the sample are always the *effective* ones — the
denominators the estimator must use.


``` r
set.seed(42)
big <- data.frame(size = rlnorm(1000, 2))
s <- chromy_sample(big, n = 100, size = "size")
s$accounting
#> $eps_sum
#> [1] 2.590029e-14
#> 
#> $corrected_unit
#> [1] 313
#> 
#> $adjusted_crossings
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $max_adjustment
#> [1] 2.58682e-14
```

## The estimator

With hits $t_i$ and effective expected hits $\lambda_i$, the multiplicity
(Hansen--Hurwitz form) estimator of a total is
$\hat{Y} = \sum_{i \in s} t_i\, y_i / \lambda_i$. It is design-unbiased
under minimum replacement, and reduces to Horvitz--Thompson when no unit
can be selected twice. For its precision no unbiased variance exists under
a systematic-like design; `estimate_total()` uses the successive-difference
estimator over the randomly decided hits, read in list order, where the
serpentine sort has left genuinely similar neighbours.

## References

Chromy, J. R. (1979). Sequential sample selection methods. *Proceedings of
the American Statistical Association, Survey Research Methods Section*,
401--406.

Chauvet, G. and Le Gleut, R. (2021). Properties of Chromy's sampling
procedure. *Survey Methodology*, 47(2), 321--347.
